# Prescriptive lessons -- van-eps x 1939-method

## maj

Van Eps treats major triads as the primary vehicle for establishing every core technical doctrine: all six fingering forms must be practiced independently and equally, with arpeggio picking (pulsation, not force) as the standard right-hand method. Legato shift governs all positional movement -- no sliding at modulation points, no rushing the final note of a measure. Finger flattening and inner-voice sustain are introduced here as the advanced demands that make balanced technique non-negotiable.

- [ch.2 p.8] Six distinct fingering forms are prescribed for harmonized major scale triads; long, medium, and condensed variants of each are practiced as separate exercises, not interchangeable shortcuts.
- [ch.2 p.9] Arpeggio picking is the core right-hand technique: the pick pulsates over each string with a slight kick, using the next-highest string as a downstroke stop. Striking two strings at once is named as the diagnostic failure of absent pulsation.
- [ch.2 p.9] (proscriptive) Forcibly pushing the pick across strings is explicitly prohibited; the two-strings-at-once error is its symptom.
- [ch.2 p.9] Equal note value is mandatory: rushing the final note of each measure to reach the next position in time is named as the characteristic error to eliminate.
- [ch.2 p.10] The sequence form -- three steps up and back on each triad, ascending then reversing -- is the structural traversal pattern governing all six forms.
- [ch.2 p.11] In mixed-rhythm exercises alternating whole-note triads with arpeggio measures, four beats must be counted for the whole-note measure exactly as for the arpeggio measure; the natural tendency to hurry the whole notes is preempted by name.
- [ch.2 p.12] The barre triad within each form is practiced with all four fingers serving as barre finger in rotation -- not only with the fingering as marked.
- [ch.2 p.13] After all six forms are perfected individually, they are joined with the octave-higher forms and practiced without a break, enabling two-octave runs through the harmonized major scale.
- [ch.2 p.14] Inner voices (half-notes below a moving melodic line) must sustain their full written value while the upper line moves; voice independence is stated as the governing purpose of practicing all three form variants for balanced technique.
- [ch.2 p.15] Finger flattening -- flattening the first joint of a fretting finger to produce an added note while that same finger sustains another -- is prescribed as a "fifth finger" maneuver requiring methodical practice and must be executed with a snap, rhythmically reliable.
- [ch.2 p.15] (proscriptive) Sliding the left hand at modulation points between forms is prohibited; the change must be a fast, accurate release lasting only a fraction of a second.
- [ch.3 p.26] Broken string-set major triad exercises require smooth pick-jumping over the skipped string; straight downstrokes precede arpeggio picking in the learning sequence.
- [ch.3 p.37] When major triad forms are transposed to lower string sets, increased fretting pressure is prescribed to compensate for string tension and obtain a clear tone.

## min

Minor triads receive the same six-form, all-keys treatment as major, with legato and unconventional fingerings as twin emphases. The method adds alternate picking (upstrokes on beats 2 and 4), bass-note sustain via extra pressure, and a retrospective full-book revision to upstrokes after downstroke mastery -- making minor the chapter where right-hand picking is generalized and systematized.

- [ch.3 p.18] Minor triad harmonized scale exercises receive the identical six-form treatment as major: arpeggio picking and all-keys transposition are the baseline; nothing is relaxed for minor.
- [ch.3 p.19] Legato is a constant, non-optional goal across all six minor fingering forms, restated as a standing requirement at each form transition.
- [ch.3 p.20] Lower minor scale forms contain unconventional but correct fingerings; the student is explicitly prohibited from substituting conventional alternatives. The forms are flagged as confusing and must be practiced with extra care precisely because of that difficulty.
- [ch.3 p.22] A tonic-triad reduction technique is prescribed: the harmonized minor scale is practiced with the tonic chord only as harmony so that each form's individual technical hazards can be isolated and addressed.
- [ch.3 p.25] Alternate picking is prescribed for minor triad harmonized scale exercises, with upstrokes assigned specifically to the second and fourth triads in each measure.
- [ch.3 p.35] When the bass note is difficult to sustain while other fingers move, extra fretting pressure on that single note -- practiced slowly -- is the prescribed remedy.
- [ch.3 p.37] Transposing minor triad forms to lower string sets requires increased fretting pressure; this is stated as a physical property of string tension, universal across chord types at lower registers.
- [ch.3 p.39] After all exercises have been learned with downstrokes, a method-wide retrospective revision is prescribed: replay every downstroke-only exercise with upstrokes alone, then with alternating strokes. Upstrokes must cross strings exactly as quickly as downstrokes.

## dim

Diminished triads are treated as the method's most technically demanding chord type, warranting the largest cluster of named techniques. The rocker-arm alternation, idle-finger suspension, four-fret symmetry jumps, open-voicing arc pick-path, and hammer-attack finger drops are all introduced here -- each with a named error that the technique is designed to prevent. Contrary-motion stretching exercises for diminished are framed as hand gymnastics, explicitly tolerating dissonance in exchange for increased finger spread.

- [ch.3 p.27] Contrary-motion diminished stretching exercises are practiced in both forms across all keys; resulting dissonances are normalized as structurally correct. Sustained practice is prescribed specifically to increase finger spread.
- [ch.3 p.28] Diminished symmetry (the chord repeats every four frets) is exploited: the same fingering is transposed in fast, slide-free positional jumps. Jumps must be fast and accurate with fingers solidly implanted; slides are the named failure.
- [ch.3 p.28] Idle fingers in diminished exercises are suspended just above -- not resting on -- the string they are not fretting. The first finger hovers above the fourth string; in the reverse exercise the fourth finger hovers above the first string. Both must lie in readiness until perfect.
- [ch.3 p.28] The rocker-arm technique is prescribed for legato diminished sequences: the first and fourth fingers alternate like the ends of a rocker arm, the first remaining down until the fourth comes down. Downstrokes are used until mastery, then alternate picking follows.
- [ch.3 p.28] (proscriptive) All four notes sounding simultaneously, even for a fraction of a second, is the diagnostic failure of incorrect rocker-arm execution and is explicitly prohibited.
- [ch.3 p.30] The fourth finger must remain arched throughout diminished exercises; the tendency to lay it flat is named as the characteristic failure mode to be actively corrected. Initial strain is acknowledged and dismissed as developmental.
- [ch.3 p.30] (proscriptive) Allowing the fourth finger to lay flat is prohibited; the arched position is the only acceptable posture regardless of the strain involved.
- [ch.3 p.30] For the unusual second-finger position in certain diminished exercises, all other fingers must remain arched while the second finger bears the strain. The same fingering ascends to the octave and reverses descending.
- [ch.3 p.31] For chromatic diminished forms requiring two successive notes from one finger, the movement must be made at maximum speed without sliding or slurring, so that the notes sound as though fingered by two separate fingers. Slow practice is prescribed as the development path.
- [ch.3 p.31] In open-voicing diminished exercises, a fretting finger simultaneously mutes the adjacent unwanted string; the second finger, for example, deadens the D string while fretting the A string note.
- [ch.3 p.32] When a sustaining voice sits above the target string in open-voicing diminished work, the pick must return via a small arc around that upper string after the downstroke so as not to stop its vibration. Complete wrist action is specified.
- [ch.3 p.32] (proscriptive) Deadening either sustaining voice with the upstroke is prohibited; the arc pick-path is the method's explicit remedy.
- [ch.3 p.34] Simultaneous two-finger drops in diminished exercises are executed hammer-fashion -- fingers pre-formed and snapped down together with the pick stroke, not merely laid down. Full note value and slow practice are required.

## 7

Seventh chord material appears narrowly in this work, limited to one structural prescription for fingerboard-range management in arpeggio exercises. The lesson is logistical rather than interpretive: the method gives a precise truncation rule rather than leaving range adaptation to the student's judgment.

- [ch.3 p.24] Seventh arpeggio exercises spanning the full fingerboard cannot be played in all keys in original form; Van Eps prescribes a specific truncation: omit the first measure when descending if the range goes too low, omit the fifth measure when ascending if it goes too high.
